Stage 03 Milestone 1.1 · Foundation

The database layer

Every table in this project gets a UUID primary key and UTC timestamps from the same three files — and Alembic has to see all of them.

app/db/base.py new app/db/session.py new migrations/env.py edit
Before you start

What you already have

Nothing new to install: all three packages came with the project setup in Stage 02. What changes here is which names you import from them — each step below carries its own hint list, folded away until you want it.

Installed in Stage 02
  • sqlalchemyThe ORM: models, queries, sessions, and the connection pool.
  • psycopgThe PostgreSQL driver that SQLAlchemy talks through.
  • alembicSchema migrations, generated by comparing your models with the database.
Step 01

Give every constraint a predictable name

Every model you write from now on will inherit from one base class, and that class carries the registry of tables Alembic compares against the real database. The registry also decides how constraints are named. Set that policy now, while there are no tables: rename a constraint later and the migration that tries to drop it won't know what it's called.

What your code has to do
  1. Create a single base class that all future models inherit from, and one table registry that belongs to it.
  2. Make constraint names deterministic: the same table and column must always produce the same name for an index, a unique constraint, a check constraint, a foreign key and a primary key. Five patterns, one per constraint type — take them from the SQLAlchemy documentation rather than inventing your own.
  3. Choose a check-constraint pattern that forces you to name each check yourself, so no unnamed check can slip into a migration.
  4. Keep this file free of settings and connections: importing a model must never require a database or a .env file.
  5. Leave it importable on its own — uv run python -c "from app.db.base import Base" must succeed before you move on.
Hint — the imports this step needs
MetaData
The table registry. It holds every table your models declare and accepts the naming convention, which is why it is created here rather than left to SQLAlchemy's default.
DeclarativeBase
The modern base class for ORM models. Subclassing it gives you typed models and lets you attach your own metadata, which the 1.x declarative_base() function made awkward.
backend/app/db/base.py 
# Deterministic names for indexes and constraints. Without them PostgreSQL
# invents names, and Alembic can't reliably alter or drop them later.
NAMING_CONVENTION: dict[str, str] = {
    "ix": "ix_%(column_0_label)s",
    "uq": "uq_%(table_name)s_%(column_0_N_name)s",
    "ck": "ck_%(table_name)s_%(constraint_name)s",
    "fk": "fk_%(table_name)s_%(column_0_N_name)s_%(referred_table_name)s",
    "pk": "pk_%(table_name)s",
}


class Base(DeclarativeBase):
    """Parent class of every ORM model.

    Its ``metadata`` collects every table declared by a subclass and applies
    ``NAMING_CONVENTION`` to their constraints, so a unique constraint on
    ``users.email`` is always named ``uq_users_email``.

    Attributes:
        metadata: Registry of all mapped tables, with the project's
            constraint naming convention.
    """

    metadata = MetaData(naming_convention=NAMING_CONVENTION)
Check yours against it
Step 02

A UUID primary key, generated in Python

Every table in this project uses a UUID primary key, and writing that column out in twelve models is twelve chances to write it differently. A mixin — a plain class a model inherits alongside Base — defines the column once.

What your code has to do
  1. Offer a reusable id column that any model can inherit without redeclaring it, stored as a native PostgreSQL UUID.
  2. Produce a fresh, unguessable value for every row — two rows created in the same run must never share an ID.
  3. Make the value available in Python before the INSERT runs, so a service can reference the new ID in the same transaction, for example when writing its audit entry.
  4. Stay a plain mixin: it must not become a table of its own, and it must not inherit from Base.
  5. Optional: arrange for id to appear as the first column in the generated CREATE TABLE.
Hint — the imports this step needs
uuid
The standard-library UUID module. uuid.uuid4 is the random generator; it is passed to the column as the callable that runs per row.
Uuid
SQLAlchemy's generic UUID column type. It becomes a native UUID on PostgreSQL and converts values to and from uuid.UUID objects for you.
Mapped
The annotation that declares an attribute's Python type. Mapped[uuid.UUID] is what tells type checkers — and SQLAlchemy — that patient.id is a UUID, not a string.
mapped_column
The database side of the same attribute. It carries the column type, primary_key, the default, and ordering options.
backend/app/db/base.py 
class UUIDPrimaryKeyMixin:
    """Adds a UUID primary key named ``id``.

    The UUID is generated in Python (``uuid.uuid4``) when the object is
    flushed, not by the database, so a service can use the new ID in the same
    transaction. Random UUIDs also keep record IDs unguessable, which supports
    the rule that out-of-scope records return 404.

    Attributes:
        id: Primary key, stored as a native PostgreSQL ``UUID``.
    """

    id: Mapped[uuid.UUID] = mapped_column(
        Uuid,
        primary_key=True,
        default=uuid.uuid4,
        sort_order=-10,
    )
Check yours against it
Step 03

Timestamps from one clock — the database's

Two columns on every table, and they only stay trustworthy if one clock sets both. An app server whose clock drifts by a few seconds can otherwise produce a row that was updated before it was created.

What your code has to do
  1. Record, for every table, when a row was created and when it last changed, as two reusable columns in a second mixin.
  2. Store both as timezone-aware UTC instants, so comparing them with datetime.now(UTC) works instead of raising TypeError.
  3. Take both values from the database's clock, not the application's — including the value written on every update.
  4. Set the creation time once, on insert; refresh the change time on every update made through the ORM.
  5. Make sure the Python object already holds the new values after an insert or update, without a follow-up query — otherwise reading updated_at after the session closes fails.
  6. Add the mapper setting that does this in a way that can't be mistaken for a column, and that Ruff won't flag as a mutable class attribute.
Hint — the imports this step needs
datetime
The Python type of both columns. Used only in the annotation, Mapped[datetime]; the values themselves are produced by PostgreSQL.
DateTime
The column type. With timezone=True it becomes TIMESTAMPTZ; without it you silently get naive timestamps.
func
A builder for SQL function calls. func.now() is not a Python value — it is SQL that the database evaluates, which is how both columns share one clock.
ClassVar
Marks an attribute as belonging to the class. Declarative mapping skips ClassVar attributes, so __mapper_args__ is not mistaken for a column.
Any
Allows mapper values of any type. It completes the annotation ClassVar[dict[str, Any]] that satisfies Ruff's RUF012.
backend/app/db/base.py 
class TimestampMixin:
    """Adds ``created_at`` and ``updated_at`` timestamps set by the database.

    Both columns are ``TIMESTAMPTZ``, so values are stored as UTC instants
    and returned as timezone-aware datetimes. A model that defines its own
    ``__mapper_args__`` replaces this one and must include
    ``"eager_defaults": True`` itself.

    Attributes:
        created_at: When the row was inserted, in UTC.
        updated_at: When the row was last changed through the ORM, in UTC.
    """

    created_at: Mapped[datetime] = mapped_column(
        DateTime(timezone=True),
        server_default=func.now(),
        sort_order=10,
    )
    updated_at: Mapped[datetime] = mapped_column(
        DateTime(timezone=True),
        server_default=func.now(),
        onupdate=func.now(),
        sort_order=10,
    )

    __mapper_args__: ClassVar[dict[str, Any]] = {"eager_defaults": True}
Check yours against it
Step 04

One engine, one session factory

The engine owns the connection pool for the whole process; the factory stamps every session with the same options. Both belong in a second file, because from here on this module is the only place that knows how to reach the database.

What your code has to do
  1. Open exactly one connection pool for the application, built from the URL in your settings — never a literal connection string in the file.
  2. Survive a database that goes to sleep: a connection handed out of the pool must be checked before it is used, so a stale one is replaced instead of raising.
  3. Keep the pool small, because the app runs a single worker and the hosted database caps connections.
  4. Ensure every connection reports timestamps in UTC, whatever the server's own timezone setting is.
  5. Produce sessions whose loaded objects stay usable after commit(), so a service can commit and still return the object it just saved.
  6. Create no tables here: schema changes belong to Alembic, so create_all must not appear anywhere.
Hint — the imports this step needs
create_engine
Builds the engine and its connection pool. Called once at import; its keyword arguments are where pooling and connection behaviour are configured.
sessionmaker
A configured factory for sessions. Options set here apply to every session, so no caller can quietly use different ones.
Session
The unit of work. Holds the identity map and the transaction; services run queries and commit through it.
get_settings
Your cached settings from Stage 02. Supplies the validated database URL, keeping credentials in the environment rather than in code.
backend/app/db/session.py 
settings = get_settings()

# pool_pre_ping replaces connections that Neon dropped while its compute was
# suspended. The pool stays small because the app runs one worker and Neon's
# free plan limits connections. Forcing the session timezone to UTC makes
# PostgreSQL return timestamps in UTC, as the API contract requires.
engine = create_engine(
    url=settings.database_url,
    pool_pre_ping=True,
    pool_size=5,
    max_overflow=5,
    connect_args={"options": "-c timezone=utc"},
)

# expire_on_commit=False keeps loaded values after commit(), so a service can
# commit and then return the object for the router to serialize.
SessionLocal = sessionmaker(
    bind=engine,
    expire_on_commit=False,
)
Check yours against it
Step 05

One session per request, always closed

FastAPI runs everything before yield when a request starts, and everything after it once the response has been sent. That makes a generator the natural shape for something that must be opened, handed over, and closed again — whatever happened in between.

What your code has to do
  1. Give each request its own session, in a shape FastAPI can inject as a dependency.
  2. Guarantee the session is closed when the request ends — including when the route raises — using exactly one cleanup mechanism, never two stacked on top of each other.
  3. Make sure work that was never committed is rolled back rather than left open on the connection.
  4. Never commit here. Committing is a service's decision: one use case, one commit.
  5. Annotate it so a reader can see it yields a session rather than returning one.
  6. Prove it: open a session, raise an error inside it, and confirm the error still reaches the caller and the session closed anyway.
Hint — the imports this step needs
Iterator
The return type of a generator function. Iterator[Session] says "this yields sessions"; Session alone would be a lie that type checkers accept.
Session
Already imported in this file. Reused here purely for the annotation.
backend/app/db/session.py 
def get_db() -> Iterator[Session]:
    """Provide one database session for the duration of a request.

    The ``with`` block closes the session in every case, including when the
    route raises, and closing rolls back any transaction that wasn't
    committed, so a failed request never leaves partial changes behind.

    Yields:
        A new ``Session`` bound to the application engine.

    Example:
        ``def list_patients(db: Annotated[Session, Depends(get_db)]): ...``
    """
    with SessionLocal() as session:
        yield session
Check yours against it
Step 06

Point Alembic at your settings and your models

alembic init left you a generic env.py that runs on every migration command. Out of the box it knows neither which database to connect to nor which tables your code declares — and one line of the template will quietly undo your work if you leave it in place.

What your code has to do
  1. Make Alembic connect using the same settings the application uses, so the URL lives in one place and alembic.ini keeps its harmless placeholder.
  2. Survive a password containing %: the value passes through configparser, which treats that character as special, so it has to be escaped.
  3. Give Alembic your models' registry to compare the database against, so autogenerate and alembic check can see tables at all.
  4. Leave exactly one assignment to that registry in the file — the template ships one of its own, and the last one wins.
  5. Keep the file tidy: imports at the top, and no leftover template comments that describe code you didn't write.
  6. Remember that a table only exists in the registry once its module has been imported, so plan where future models get imported.
Hint — the imports this step needs
get_settings
The application settings. Importing them here is what keeps the database URL — and its password — out of alembic.ini and out of Git.
Base
Your declarative base from Step 01. Its metadata is the model side of every comparison Alembic makes.
context
Already in the template. context.config is the object holding the values read from alembic.ini, and it is what you override.
backend/migrations/env.py 
# Alembic config object, giving access to the values in alembic.ini.
config = context.config

settings = get_settings()
# configparser treats "%" as special, so escape it in case the password contains one.
config.set_main_option("sqlalchemy.url", settings.database_url.replace("%", "%%"))

# Tables appear in Base.metadata only after their models module is imported,
# so every new models module must be imported in this file.
target_metadata = Base.metadata

Finish

Check your work

Run both from backend/, with the database container up (docker compose up -d db). The first proves the connection and the UTC setting; the second proves Alembic can reach the database and read your metadata.

backend/
uv run python -c "from app.db.session import engine; from sqlalchemy import text; print(engine.connect().execute(text('show timezone')).scalar())"
UTC
backend/
uv run alembic check
INFO [alembic.runtime.migration] Context impl PostgresqlImpl. INFO [alembic.runtime.migration] Will assume transactional DDL.
No new upgrade operations detected.

There are no models yet, so "no new upgrade operations" is the correct answer here: the database and Base.metadata agree because both are empty. The first real table arrives in the next stage, and this same command will then tell you when a migration is missing.
